name: Byzantine Empire
summary: The continuation of the Roman Empire in the east, centred on Constantinople, which lasted more than a thousand years until the Ottoman conquest in 1453.

knownFor.label: Hagia Sophia
knownFor.note: Its dome was the largest for nearly a thousand years.

knownFor.label: Greek fire
knownFor.note: A liquid incendiary weapon used at sea.

knownFor.label: Byzantine silk
knownFor.note: Silkworm eggs were smuggled from Asia around 552.

location.value: The eastern Mediterranean, centred on Constantinople. At its greatest extent (565) under Justinian I it held Italy, North Africa, Egypt, the Levant, Anatolia and the Balkans.

terrain.value: Constantinople stood on a defensible peninsula controlling the Bosporus between Europe and Asia, protected by sea walls and the Theodosian land walls.
terrain.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

climate.value: Mediterranean. A cold period after volcanic eruptions in 536 CE coincided with plague and hardship in the 6th century.
climate.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

resources.value: Egyptian grain (until the 640s), Anatolian farmland, silk production (after silkworms were smuggled in, c. 550s), and trade tolls.
resources.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

disasters.value: The Plague of Justinian began around 541 and recurred for two centuries. Earthquakes struck Constantinople several times.

population.value: About 27 million in 540, 12 million in 800, 18 million in 1025, 3–5 million in 1282, and 2 million in 1312 (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Constantinople was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe until the 13th century (perhaps 400,000–500,000 people at its height), but shrank to about 50,000 by 1453.

disease.value: The Plague of Justinian (from 541) killed a large share of the population. The Black Death struck in 1347.

migration.value: Slavs, Bulgars and later Turks settled in former Byzantine lands. Armenians and others served and settled within the empire.
migration.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

economicBase.value: Agriculture, craft industries (silk), and trade through Constantinople, with strong state regulation (the Book of the Eparch).

tradeRoutes.value: Constantinople linked the Black Sea, Mediterranean and Silk Road routes. Venetian and Genoese merchants won major trading privileges from the 11th century.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate is given in the sources checked. Losses to the Arabs in the 7th century cost it as much as three-quarters of its revenue.

moneyAndTax.value: The gold solidus (introduced by Constantine) was a stable international currency for centuries, later replaced by the hyperpyron (1092). Land taxes funded the army.

inequality.value: Large landowners (dynatoi) grew at the expense of free peasant-soldiers, which emperors such as Basil II tried to limit.
inequality.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

governmentType.value: An absolute monarchy under an emperor seen as God’s representative, with a large salaried bureaucracy and close ties to the Orthodox Church.

keyRulers.value: Constantine I (founded Constantinople, 330). Justinian I (527–565). Heraclius (610–641). Basil II (976–1025). Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118). Constantine XI (1449–1453, last).

succession.value: No fixed law. Dynasties ruled, but emperors were often overthrown by coups, blinding or murder. Usurpation was a routine route to the throne.
succession.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

institutions.value: Roman law codified by Justinian (the Corpus Juris Civilis, 529–534), the themes (military provinces), the Senate, and the Patriarch of Constantinople.

stability.value: The Nika riots (532). Repeated civil wars. The Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople (1204), which split the empire. Civil wars in the 14th century.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between military aristocrats and the civil court, and between factions over religion (e.g. the Iconoclasm controversy, 8th–9th centuries).

armyAndTech.value: Professional armies of about 150,000+ in the 6th century, falling to under 8,000 defenders in 1453. “Greek fire”, a secret incendiary weapon, saved Constantinople from Arab fleets (670s, 717–718).

majorWars.value: Justinian’s reconquests (530s–550s). The Byzantine–Sasanian War (602–628). The Arab conquests (630s–640s). The Battle of Manzikert (1071). The Fourth Crusade (1204). The Ottoman siege of 1453.

territoryChange.value: Greatest extent in 565. Lost Syria and Egypt to the Arabs (630s–640s). Recovered under Basil II (by 1025, from the Danube to the Euphrates). Shrank to Constantinople and a few lands by the 15th century.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Sasanian Persia, the Caliphates, the Bulgarians, the Seljuks, the Normans, Venice and the Ottomans. It used diplomacy, tribute and marriage alliances skilfully.

inventions.value: Greek fire, the dome engineering of Hagia Sophia (537), and preservation of Greek science and medicine.

scienceEducation.value: Preserved classical Greek learning. The University of Constantinople (Magnaura school). Byzantine scholars carried Greek texts to Renaissance Italy.
scienceEducation.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

openness.value: Culturally confident and influential, but often wary of the Latin West, especially after the Crusades.
openness.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

communicationTransport.value: Roman roads and a state post; a strong navy and merchant shipping on the Mediterranean and Black Sea; fire-beacon signals across Anatolia (9th century).

religion.value: Christianity became the state religion under Theodosius I. Eastern Orthodox Christianity separated from Rome in the East–West Schism (1054).

languageWriting.value: Greek. Latin was used officially until the 6th century, after which Greek replaced it.

artsArchitecture.value: Hagia Sophia, mosaics (Ravenna, Constantinople), icons, and illuminated manuscripts.

socialStructure.value: Emperor, aristocracy, clergy and monks, townspeople, and free and dependent peasants. Slavery was legal but declining.

sharedIdentity.value: Its people called themselves Romans (Rhomaioi) and their state Rhomania. “Byzantine” is a later Western label.

dailyLife.value: Stone and brick houses, often several storeys in Constantinople; bread, olive oil, fish, wine and cheese.

neighbours.value: Persia, the Arabs, Bulgaria, Kievan Rus’, Venice, the Crusader states, the Seljuks and the Ottomans.

ideasReligions.value: Spread Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet to the Slavs (Bulgaria, Serbia, Rus’). Preserved Roman law and Greek learning for Europe.
ideasReligions.source: Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

colonisation.value: A Roman imperial state rather than a coloniser. It lost territory to conquerors over time.

riseSignals.value: Continued the Roman Empire in the richer, more urban east after the West fell, protected by Constantinople’s location and walls.

peakPeriod.value: Justinian I (greatest extent, 565). A second high point under Basil II (976–1025).

declineSignals.value: Plague, the Persian wars and the Arab conquests (7th century). Manzikert (1071). The crusader sack of 1204. Civil wars and loss of revenue.

outcome.value: Conquest. The Ottomans captured Constantinople on 29 May 1453, and it became their capital.

sources.value: Byzantine historians (Procopius, Anna Komnene), legal codes, seals, coins, and Arab and Latin sources. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Treadgold (1997).

overallCertainty.value: Good for political events. When to start the “Byzantine” period (330, 395, or the 7th century) is a convention. Population figures are estimates from different historians.
